      <title>The AI Race Has a Missing Question: Can We Explain What Our Agents Already Did?</title>
      <dc:creator>Srinivas Kondepudi</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 16:08:34 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/sirinivask/the-ai-race-has-a-missing-question-can-we-explain-what-our-agents-already-did-4l03</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/sirinivask/the-ai-race-has-a-missing-question-can-we-explain-what-our-agents-already-did-4l03</guid>
      <description><p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fjqly1fv0ca4jc4l6mp6m.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Fjqly1fv0ca4jc4l6mp6m.png" alt="Chron" width="799" height="441"></a></p>

<p>The public conversation around advanced AI often collapses into two positions.</p>

<p>One side says we should slow down.</p>

<p>The other says progress is inevitable, so we should accelerate and compete.</p>

<p>Both arguments matter. But teams deploying AI agents today face a more immediate problem:</p>

<p><strong>Can we explain what the agents already did inside our own environments?</strong></p>

<p>That question is less dramatic than the future of superintelligence. It is also more operationally urgent.</p>

<p>AI coding assistants and autonomous agents are no longer limited to suggesting text in a chat window. They can inspect repositories, execute commands, call tools, modify files, use credentials, interact with ticketing systems, and reach external services.</p>

<p>Once that happens, "we have a policy" is no longer enough.</p>

<p>A team needs to be able to answer basic questions after an incident, review, or audit:</p>

<ul>
<li>What was the original request?</li>
<li>Which tools did the agent use?</li>
<li>What happened between the prompt and the final answer?</li>
<li>Which files or systems were changed?</li>
<li>Was a risky action approved?</li>
<li>Did a person review the result?</li>
<li>Can someone else reconstruct the sequence later?</li>
</ul>

<p>The important word is not logging. It is <strong>causality</strong>.</p>

<p>A repository might show that a file changed. A chat transcript might show that someone asked for help. An access log might show that a credential was used.</p>

<p>But those records often do not explain how the events connect:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>Which agent action led to this command, which led to this file write, under which user request, with which approval?</p>
</blockquote>

<p>That missing chain is where accountability disappears.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  This is not an argument for blocking every action
</h2>

<p>Human checkpoints matter, especially for irreversible or high-impact actions. But prompting a person for approval on every operation creates its own failure mode: approval fatigue.</p>

<p>Anthropic has written publicly about this tradeoff. Its experience with agent permissions found that people approved the overwhelming majority of prompts, making constant confirmation an unreliable safety mechanism by itself. Their focus is increasingly on technical containment: constraining what an agent can do through boundaries such as sandboxes, virtual machines, and egress controls. Read Anthropic's discussion.</p>

<p>The point is not to eliminate human review.</p>

<p>It is to reserve it for the moments where it matters, then preserve evidence that the review happened.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Governance needs two layers
</h2>

<p>A useful operating model has two distinct layers.</p>

<p><strong>Preventive controls</strong> constrain what an agent can do: scoped credentials, network boundaries, sandboxes, policy enforcement, and approval gates.</p>

<p><strong>Detective controls</strong> preserve what the agent did: requests, tool calls, results, files changed, timestamps, decisions, approvals, and evidence of review.</p>

<p>One without the other is incomplete.</p>

<p>Preventive controls can reduce harm, but they cannot explain an action later unless the decision itself is recorded.</p>

<p>Logs can support an investigation, but they cannot prevent an agent from reaching a system it should never have been allowed to access.</p>

<p>This is why the conversation should not be "governance versus innovation." Good governance is part of what lets teams adopt useful agents with confidence.</p>

<p>OpenAI's own discussion of safely operating coding agents describes the same ingredients: technical boundaries, approval decisions, agent-aware telemetry, and the ability to inspect the original request, tool activity, results, and policy decisions when something needs review. Read OpenAI's approach.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Build the evidence trail before you need it
</h2>

<p>The worst time to ask how an AI agent acted is after something went wrong.</p>

<p>By then, the prompt may be gone, the context may have been compacted, tool output may have changed, and the person who ran the session may not remember why a decision was made.</p>

<p>Evidence is cheap to preserve at the moment of action and expensive to reconstruct later.</p>

<p>That is the problem Chron is built around.</p>

<p>Chron is a local-first audit trail for AI-assisted work. It records AI sessions and their events, maintains evidence integrity locally, and helps teams find the sessions that warrant review. It does not certify compliance or replace a human auditor. It gives teams a more defensible starting point: a record of what occurred.</p>

<p>The argument about how quickly AI should progress will continue.</p>

<p>In the meantime, organizations should make sure that the AI already acting in their codebases and environments is not operating in a black box.</p>

<p>Because the question after an incident will not be:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>"Was the model powerful?"</p>
</blockquote>

<p>It will be:</p>

<blockquote>
<p>"What did it do?"</p>
</blockquote>

</p>

</code></pre>

      <title>Authentication vs Authorization: The Two Most-Confused Words in Security</title>
      <dc:creator>Sri Balaji</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 14:43:04 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/sri2614/authentication-vs-authorization-the-two-most-confused-words-in-security-1l03</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/sri2614/authentication-vs-authorization-the-two-most-confused-words-in-security-1l03</guid>
      <description><blockquote>
<p>⚡ <strong>TL;DR:</strong> Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you can do. Run them in that order, carry identity with sessions or tokens, and put each check in the right place. Confuse the two and you ship security holes.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2>
  
  
  Contents
</h2>

<ul>
<li>Same prefix, completely different jobs</li>
<li>Two questions, in order</li>
<li>Where each check lives in a request</li>
<li>Sessions vs tokens: how identity is carried</li>
<li>OAuth and OIDC, without the jargon</li>
<li>In code: verify identity, then check permission</li>
<li>Common mistakes that ship security holes</li>
<li>Takeaways</li>
<li>Where to go next</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Same prefix, completely different jobs
</h2>

<p>You add a login page, users sign in, and you breathe out. The app feels secure. Then a junior engineer signs in with their own valid account, changes the URL from <code>/orders/42</code> to <code>/orders/43</code>, and sees someone else's invoice. Nothing was "hacked", every request had a valid session. The login worked perfectly. The problem was never login at all.</p>

<p>That gap is the difference between <strong>authentication</strong> and <strong>authorization</strong>. They share a prefix, they sit next to each other in the request, and they get used interchangeably in standups, which is exactly why people ship the bug above. Once you can keep them apart in your head, a huge class of security mistakes simply stops happening.</p>

<blockquote>
<p>📌 <strong>Who this is for:</strong> Developers who can build a login form but get fuzzy on what happens after sign-in. If you have ever wondered "is this a 401 or a 403?", written an <code>if (user.isAdmin)</code> check in a React component, or copy-pasted JWT verification without quite knowing what it proves, this is for you. No prior security background needed.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2>
  
  
  Two questions, in order
</h2>

<blockquote>
<p>Authentication (authn) answers "who are you?", it proves identity. Authorization (authz) answers "what are you allowed to do?", it grants or denies access to a specific action or resource. Authn always runs first; authz depends on its answer.</p>
</blockquote>

<p>Notice the ordering. You cannot decide what someone is allowed to do until you know who they are. But knowing who they are tells you nothing, on its own, about what they may do. Those are two separate decisions, made at two separate moments, often by two separate parts of your system.</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>In the real world</th>
<th>In tech</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Showing your passport at the security checkpoint</td>
<td>Authentication, the system confirms you are who you claim to be</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Your boarding pass says seat 14C on flight BA42 today</td>
<td>Authorization, you may board THIS flight, in THIS seat, right now</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A valid passport does not let you board any plane you want</td>
<td>Being authenticated does not mean you are authorized for an action</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>The lounge agent re-checks your pass at the gate</td>
<td>Authorization is re-checked at each protected resource, not just once</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p><em>The airport makes the split obvious, two checkpoints, two different questions.</em></p>

<p>Your passport is real whether you are flying to Tokyo or standing in a parking lot, identity is stable. The boarding pass is scoped: one flight, one seat, one day. That scoping is the whole point of authorization, and it is why "they logged in" is never a complete answer to "should they be able to do this?".</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Where each check lives in a request
</h2>

<p>Every protected request runs the same gauntlet. The client presents a credential, the server verifies it to establish identity, then a separate step asks whether that identity may perform this exact action on this exact resource. Only if both pass does your business logic ever run.</p>

<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fmermaid.ink%2Fimg%-QWxsb3dlZCBmb3IgdGhpcz8iKQogIGNsYXNzIG5fYXV0aHogY29tcHV0ZTsKICBuX2hhbmRsZXIoIkhhbmRsZXI8YnIvPkJ1c2luZXNzIGxvZ2ljIikKICBjbGFzcyBuX2hhbmRsZXIgY29tcHV0ZTsKICBuX3N0b3JlKCJJZGVudGl0eSAvIFBvbGljeTxici8-dXNlcnMsIHJvbGVzLCBzY29wZXMiKQogIGNsYXNzIG5fc3RvcmUgZGF0YTsKICBuX3JlamVjdCgiNDAxIC8gNDAzPGJyLz5yZWplY3RlZCBlYXJseSIpCiAgY2xhc3Mgbl9yZWplY3QgZXh0ZXJuYWw7CiAgbl9jbGllbnQgLS0-fCJ0b2tlbiAvIGNvb2tpZSJ8IG5fYXV0aG4KICBuX2F1dGhuIC0tPnwiaWRlbnRpdHkifCBuX2F1dGh6CiAgbl9hdXRoeiAtLT58InBlcm1pdHRlZCJ8IG5faGFuZGxlcgogIG5fc3RvcmUgLS4tPiBuX2F1dGhuCiAgbl9zdG9yZSAtLi0-IG5fYXV0aHoKICBuX2F1dGhuIC0uLT58Im5vL2ludmFsaWQgY3JlZHMgKDQwMSkifCBuX3JlamVjdAogIG5fYXV0aHogLS4tPnwibm90IGFsbG93ZWQgKDQwMykifCBuX3JlamVjdA%3FbgColor%3D0d1017%26type%3Dpng" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fmermaid.ink%2Fimg%-QWxsb3dlZCBmb3IgdGhpcz8iKQogIGNsYXNzIG5fYXV0aHogY29tcHV0ZTsKICBuX2hhbmRsZXIoIkhhbmRsZXI8YnIvPkJ1c2luZXNzIGxvZ2ljIikKICBjbGFzcyBuX2hhbmRsZXIgY29tcHV0ZTsKICBuX3N0b3JlKCJJZGVudGl0eSAvIFBvbGljeTxici8-dXNlcnMsIHJvbGVzLCBzY29wZXMiKQogIGNsYXNzIG5fc3RvcmUgZGF0YTsKICBuX3JlamVjdCgiNDAxIC8gNDAzPGJyLz5yZWplY3RlZCBlYXJseSIpCiAgY2xhc3Mgbl9yZWplY3QgZXh0ZXJuYWw7CiAgbl9jbGllbnQgLS0-fCJ0b2tlbiAvIGNvb2tpZSJ8IG5fYXV0aG4KICBuX2F1dGhuIC0tPnwiaWRlbnRpdHkifCBuX2F1dGh6CiAgbl9hdXRoeiAtLT58InBlcm1pdHRlZCJ8IG5faGFuZGxlcgogIG5fc3RvcmUgLS4tPiBuX2F1dGhuCiAgbl9zdG9yZSAtLi0-IG5fYXV0aHoKICBuX2F1dGhuIC0uLT58Im5vL2ludmFsaWQgY3JlZHMgKDQwMSkifCBuX3JlamVjdAogIG5fYXV0aHogLS4tPnwibm90IGFsbG93ZWQgKDQwMykifCBuX3JlamVjdA%3FbgColor%3D0d1017%26type%3Dpng" alt="One request, two gates: authenticate (who), then authorize (allowed for this action?), then the handler runs." width="1007" height="230"></a></p>

<p><em>One request, two gates: authenticate (who), then authorize (allowed for this action?), then the handler runs.</em></p>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Client sends a credential</strong>: A request arrives carrying proof of identity, a session cookie, a bearer JWT in the Authorization header, or an API key. No credential at all means the request is anonymous.</li>
<li>
<strong>Authenticate: who are you?</strong>: The server validates the credential, verifies the JWT signature and expiry, or looks up the session ID in its store. Success yields a trusted identity (a user id, maybe roles/scopes). Failure returns 401 Unauthorized and stops here.</li>
<li>
<strong>Authorize: allowed for THIS?</strong>: Now that identity is known, a policy check asks whether this user may perform this specific action on this specific resource, not "are they logged in" but "may user 42 delete order 43?". Failure returns 403 Forbidden.</li>
<li>
<strong>Handler runs</strong>: Only after both gates pass does the actual business logic execute. By the time your handler runs, identity is proven and the action is permitted, the handler should not have to re-litigate either.</li>
</ol>

<blockquote>
<p>💡 <strong>Tip:</strong> The two failure codes map cleanly: <strong>401 Unauthorized</strong> means "I don't know who you are" (authn failed, go log in). <strong>403 Forbidden</strong> means "I know exactly who you are, and you still can't do this" (authz failed, logging in again won't help). Despite its name, 401 is the authentication error.</p>
</blockquote>

<h2>
  
  
  Sessions vs tokens: how identity is carried
</h2>

<p>Authentication does not stop after login, proof of identity has to ride along on every subsequent request, because HTTP is stateless. There are two dominant ways to carry it, and they make opposite trade-offs.</p>

<p><strong>Sessions</strong> are server-side. After login the server creates a session record (in memory, Redis, or a database) and hands the client an opaque session ID in a cookie. Every request sends the cookie; the server looks the ID up to recover the identity. The token itself carries no information, it is just a key into server state. Revoking access is trivial: delete the row.</p>

<p><strong>Tokens</strong> (typically JWTs) are self-contained. After login the server signs a token that embeds the claims, user id, roles, expiry, and the client sends it on each request. The server verifies the signature and trusts the contents without a lookup, which scales beautifully across many services. The catch: a signed token is valid until it expires, so you cannot easily revoke one mid-flight. That is why access tokens should be short-lived and paired with a refresh token.</p>

<div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Dimension</th>
<th>Server sessions</th>
<th>JWT / tokens</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Where state lives</td>
<td>Server (store / DB)</td>
<td>Inside the token itself</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Lookup per request</td>
<td>Yes, fetch the session</td>
<td>No, verify the signature</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Revocation</td>
<td>Instant (delete the record)</td>
<td>Hard until expiry; needs a denylist</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Scales across services</td>
<td>Needs shared session store</td>
<td>Naturally, any service can verify</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Best lifetime</td>
<td>Long-ish, revocable</td>
<td>Short access + refresh token</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Carried in</td>
<td>Cookie (HttpOnly)</td>
<td>Authorization: Bearer header</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>

<p><em>Sessions vs tokens, the trade-off is statefulness vs revocability.</em></p>

<h2>
  
  
  OAuth and OIDC, without the jargon
</h2>

<p>Two more terms get tangled into the authn/authz knot, so let us untangle them in one breath. <strong>OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework</strong>, it lets a user grant one app limited access to their data in another app without sharing a password. When you click "Connect your Google Calendar", OAuth is what issues an access token scoped to just your calendar.</p>

<p><strong>OIDC (OpenID Connect) is an authentication layer built on top of OAuth.</strong> It adds an <code>id_token</code>, a JWT that proves who the user is, so apps can use "Sign in with Google" for login, not just data access. Rule of thumb: OAuth = delegated authorization (access to resources); OIDC = federated authentication (proof of identity). Most "Sign in with X" buttons are OIDC; most "Allow X to access your Y" consent screens are OAuth scopes.</p>

<p>The <strong>scopes</strong> you see on those consent screens (<code>read:calendar</code>, <code>email</code>, <code>profile</code>) are authorization data riding inside an authentication flow. Your app should treat scopes as one input to its own policy decisions, not as the final word on what a user may do inside your system.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  In code: verify identity, then check permission
</h2>

<p>Here is the whole idea in one Python handler. The first block proves identity from a JWT (authentication). The second block, a completely separate decision, asks whether that proven identity may act on this particular resource (authorization). Keep them visibly distinct.</p>

<p><code>orders_api.py</code><br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight python"><code><span class="kn">import</span> <span class="n">jwt</span>  <span class="c1"># PyJWT
</span><span class="kn">from</span> <span class="n">fastapi</span> <span class="kn">import</span> <span class="n">HTTPException</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">Request</span>

<span class="n">JWT_SECRET</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">...load-from-env...</span><span class="sh">"</span>

<span class="c1"># --- AUTHENTICATION: who are you? ---
</span><span class="k">def</span> <span class="nf">authenticate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">Request</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nb">dict</span><span class="p">:</span>
    <span class="n">header</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">request</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">headers</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Authorization</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="sh">""</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="ow">not</span> <span class="n">header</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">startswith</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Bearer </span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">):</span>
        <span class="c1"># No credential at all -&gt; we don't know who you are.
</span>        <span class="k">raise</span> <span class="nc">HTTPException</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">status_code</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">401</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">detail</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Missing token</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="n">token</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">header</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">removeprefix</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Bearer </span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="k">try</span><span class="p">:</span>
        <span class="c1"># Verifies signature AND expiry. Returns the claims if valid.
</span>        <span class="n">claims</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">jwt</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">decode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">token</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">JWT_SECRET</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">algorithms</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">HS256</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">])</span>
    <span class="k">except</span> <span class="n">jwt</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">InvalidTokenError</span><span class="p">:</span>
        <span class="k">raise</span> <span class="nc">HTTPException</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">status_code</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">401</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">detail</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Invalid token</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">claims</span>  <span class="c1"># e.g. {"sub": "42", "roles": ["customer"]}
</span>

<span class="c1"># --- AUTHORIZATION: are you allowed to do THIS? ---
</span><span class="k">def</span> <span class="nf">authorize_order_access</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">user</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">dict</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="bp">None</span><span class="p">:</span>
    <span class="n">is_owner</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">customer_id</span> <span class="o">==</span> <span class="n">user</span><span class="p">[</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">sub</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">]</span>
    <span class="n">is_admin</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">admin</span><span class="sh">"</span> <span class="ow">in</span> <span class="n">user</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">get</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">roles</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="p">[])</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="ow">not</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="n">is_owner</span> <span class="ow">or</span> <span class="n">is_admin</span><span class="p">):</span>
        <span class="c1"># We know exactly who you are -- you still can't have this.
</span>        <span class="k">raise</span> <span class="nc">HTTPException</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">status_code</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">403</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">detail</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="s">Forbidden</span><span class="sh">"</span><span class="p">)</span>


<span class="k">async</span> <span class="k">def</span> <span class="nf">get_order</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="n">Request</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">order_id</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nb">str</span><span class="p">):</span>
    <span class="n">user</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">authenticate</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">request</span><span class="p">)</span>              <span class="c1"># 1. prove identity
</span>    <span class="n">order</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="k">await</span> <span class="n">db</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">orders</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nf">find</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">order_id</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="k">if</span> <span class="n">order</span> <span class="ow">is</span> <span class="bp">None</span><span class="p">:</span>
        <span class="k">raise</span> <span class="nc">HTTPException</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">status_code</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="mi">404</span><span class="p">)</span>
    <span class="nf">authorize_order_access</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">user</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">order</span><span class="p">)</span>        <span class="c1"># 2. check permission
</span>    <span class="k">return</span> <span class="n">order</span>                               <span class="c1"># 3. only now: business logic
</span></code></pre>

</div>



<p>The authorization check is <strong>resource-scoped</strong>: it compares the resource's owner against the caller. That is what stops the <code>/orders/43</code> attack from the intro, a valid token authenticates the attacker, but they are not the owner, so <code>authorize_order_access</code> returns 403. The bug at the top of this article is exactly an app that ran step 1 and skipped step 2.</p>

<p>This pattern of "is the caller the owner, or do they have a role that overrides it?" is <strong>RBAC</strong> (role-based access control). When rules get richer, "managers can refund orders under €500 in their own region", you graduate to <strong>ABAC</strong> (attribute-based access control), where the decision is a function of attributes of the user, the resource, and the context. Same place in the request; just a more expressive policy.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Common mistakes that ship security holes
</h2>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Assuming authentication implies authorization.</strong> "They're logged in" is not "they may do this." Every protected action needs its own permission check against the specific resource, the single most common real-world breach (broken object-level authorization, the <code>/orders/43</code> bug).</li>
<li>
<strong>Enforcing authorization only in the UI.</strong> Hiding the Delete button for non-admins is UX, not security. The endpoint is still reachable with curl. Every check that hides a button in the frontend must be re-enforced on the server, where it cannot be bypassed.</li>
<li>
<strong>Long-lived or non-revocable tokens.</strong> A JWT with a 30-day expiry and no denylist means a leaked token is a 30-day master key. Keep access tokens short (minutes), use refresh tokens, and have a revocation path for the cases that matter.</li>
<li>
<strong>Trusting claims you didn't verify.</strong> Decoding a JWT is not verifying it. Always check the signature and expiry (and issuer/audience) before trusting a single claim, an unverified <code>"roles": ["admin"]</code> is just attacker-supplied JSON.</li>
<li>
<strong>Checking permissions far from the resource.</strong> Authorization decided at the gateway with stale role data can drift from reality. Decide as close to the protected resource as you can, with current data.</li>
</ol>

<h2>
  
  
  Takeaways
</h2>

<p><strong>The whole article in seven lines</strong></p>

<ul>
<li>Authentication = who are you. Authorization = what may you do. Authn runs first; authz depends on it.</li>
<li>401 = I don't know you (authn failed). 403 = I know you and you still can't (authz failed).</li>
<li>Sessions store state on the server (easy revoke); tokens carry state in the JWT (easy scale, hard revoke).</li>
<li>OAuth = delegated authorization (resource access). OIDC = authentication on top of OAuth (proof of identity).</li>
<li>Authorization must be resource-scoped: not "are you logged in" but "may YOU touch THIS".</li>
<li>Always enforce authorization on the server, UI hiding is not security.</li>
<li>Short-lived tokens, verify signatures, decide permissions close to the resource.</li>
</ul>

<h2>
  
  
  Where to go next
</h2>

<p>Authn and authz are the spine of every secure system, but they live inside a bigger picture. Two natural next steps: see how these checks fit into a hardened API surface, and how identity stops being a one-time gate and becomes a continuous decision.</p>

<ul>
<li>
<a href="https://thesimplifiedtech.com/blog/secure-api-design" rel="noopener noreferrer">Secure API Design</a>, where authn/authz sit among input validation, rate limiting, and safe defaults.</li>
<li>
<a href="https://thesimplifiedtech.com/blog/zero-trust-networking-beginners" rel="noopener noreferrer">Zero Trust Networking for Beginners</a>, "never trust, always verify": authorization re-checked on every hop, not just at the edge.</li>
<li>
<a href="https://thesimplifiedtech.com/career-paths/devops-engineer" rel="noopener noreferrer">DevOps Engineer path</a>, the role track where securing services and pipelines is part of the day job.</li>
</ul>

      <title>Stopping Rogue Deployments: How I Programmed Azure API Guardrails to Protect the Cloud Wallet</title>
      <dc:creator>Abhishek Kadlii</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 09:49:58 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/abhishek_kadlii_9ef4ca8bc/stopping-rogue-deployments-how-i-programmed-azure-api-guardrails-to-protect-the-cloud-wallet-340m</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/abhishek_kadlii_9ef4ca8bc/stopping-rogue-deployments-how-i-programmed-azure-api-guardrails-to-protect-the-cloud-wallet-340m</guid>
      <description><p>Every cloud architect knows the sudden wave of anxiety that comes with opening a billing dashboard and seeing an unexpected cost spike. In large enterprise environments, these spikes rarely happen due to malicious attacks—they happen due to human error. A junior developer spinning up a high-performance compute or GPU node for a minor test case and forgetting to deprovision it over the weekend can vaporize a sandbox budget in hours.</p>

<p>Instead of relying on warning emails, training manuals, or reactive cleanup scripts, I stepped up as a DevSecOps engineer to solve this problem at the source. I programmed the <strong>Azure Resource Manager (ARM) API gateway</strong> itself to automatically intercept and decline unauthorized resource allocations using <strong>Azure Policy</strong> and <strong>Custom RBAC Least-Privilege roles</strong>.</p>




<h3>
  
  
  🏰 The Analogy: The Bouncing Corporate Credit Card
</h3>

<p>To understand this architecture, look at how corporate spending is managed in the physical world:</p>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>The Weak Setup (The Honor System):</strong> Handing a corporate credit card with a ₹5,00,000 limit to an employee, giving them a policy handbook, and hoping they do not buy a luxury watch. If they make a mistake, the money is already gone, and you are left doing damage control.</li>
<li>  <strong>The Guardrail Setup (The Terminal Lock):</strong> Programming the payment terminal directly at the cash register. If the employee attempts to swipe the card for anything outside approved inventory codes or locations, the transaction is forcefully declined on the spot before a single rupee leaves the corporate account.
</li>
</ul>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>                               ┌──► [ Approved SKU: B-Series Only ] ──► ✅ ALLOWED (Passes Gate)
                               │
[ Deployment Request ] ──► [ Azure Policy ARM Gate ]
                               │
                               └──► [ Prohibited SKU: D-Series Node ] ──► ❌ DENIED (Declined at Register)
</code></pre>

</div>






<h3>
  
  
  🛠️ The Step-by-Step Command-Line Execution Blueprint
</h3>

<p>To demonstrate a production-grade governance implementation, I configured the deployment ring via the Azure CLI inside the <strong>Southeast Asia</strong> datacenter region using an isolated sandbox perimeter scope:</p>

<h4>
  
  
  1. Designing the Custom Policy Criteria (<code>allowed-skus.json</code>)
</h4>

<p>I engineered a strict JSON rule block that targets virtual machine resources, setting the active evaluation flag to a forceful <code>deny</code> effect if the requested hardware profile falls outside of approved low-cost shapes:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"if"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"allOf"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
      </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"field"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"type"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"equals"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines"</span><span class="w">
      </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">
      </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"field"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/sku.name"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="nl">"notIn"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
          </span><span class="s2">"Standard_B1s"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
          </span><span class="s2">"Standard_B2ats_v2"</span><span class="w">
        </span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
      </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="p">},</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"then"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="nl">"effect"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"deny"</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span></code></pre>

</div>



<h4>
  
  
  2. Provisioning and Binding the Policy Scope
</h4>

<p>I initialized the baseline target resource group perimeter and registered the schema with the control plane, passing metadata parameters as explicit flags to satisfy the Azure CLI parser rules:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code><span class="c"># Initialize the target perimeter container</span>
az group create <span class="nt">--name</span> <span class="s2">"Marathahalli_Lab_RG"</span> <span class="nt">--location</span> <span class="s2">"southeastasia"</span>

<span class="c"># Register the core custom definition rule container</span>
az policy definition create <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--name</span> <span class="s2">"restrict-vm-skus"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--display-name</span> <span class="s2">"Restrict VM SKUs to B-Series"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--rules</span> allowed-skus.json <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--mode</span> <span class="s2">"Indexed"</span>

<span class="c"># Assign the policy enforcer live to the specific Resource Group scope</span>
az policy assignment create <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--name</span> <span class="s2">"Enforce_B_Series_Only"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--policy</span> <span class="s2">"restrict-vm-skus"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--display-name</span> <span class="s2">"Enforce B-Series Only"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--resource-group</span> <span class="s2">"Marathahalli_Lab_RG"</span>
</code></pre>

</div>






<h3>
  
  
  ⚙️ Forging a Custom Least-Privilege RBAC Identity Role
</h3>

<p>Governance is incomplete without identity isolation. Instead of granting wide open contributor rights, I constructed a tailored JSON permission schema (<code>vm-operator-role.json</code>) defining a custom <strong><code>VM Restart Operator</code></strong> role. This role explicitly limits identity capabilities to virtual machine visibility and reboot actions, leaving write actions, configurations changes, and resource deletions sealed shut.<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"Name"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"VM Restart Operator"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"IsCustom"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"Description"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="s2">"Can only read and restart virtual machines inside the environment."</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"Actions"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="s2">"Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/read"</span><span class="p">,</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="s2">"Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/restart/action"</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="p">],</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"NotActions"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[],</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="nl">"AssignableScopes"</span><span class="p">:</span><span class="w"> </span><span class="p">[</span><span class="w">
    </span><span class="s2">"/subscriptions/YOUR_SUBSCRIPTION_ID"</span><span class="w">
  </span><span class="p">]</span><span class="w">
</span><span class="p">}</span><span class="w">
</span></code></pre>

</div>



<p>I programmatically extracted the subscription context and registered the custom RBAC identity blueprint live with the Azure identity control plane API:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code><span class="c"># Dynamically fetch current active subscription ID text string</span>
<span class="nv">SUB_ID</span><span class="o">=</span><span class="si">$(</span>az account show <span class="nt">--query</span> <span class="nb">id</span> <span class="nt">--output</span> tsv<span class="si">)</span>

<span class="c"># Inject the active subscription path into our assignable scopes payload</span>
<span class="nb">sed</span> <span class="nt">-i</span> <span class="s2">"s|YOUR_SUBSCRIPTION_ID|</span><span class="nv">$SUB_ID</span><span class="s2">|g"</span> vm-operator-role.json

<span class="c"># Register the custom RBAC identity blueprint live in the active directory tenant</span>
az role definition create <span class="nt">--role-definition</span> vm-operator-role.json
</code></pre>

</div>






<h3>
  
  
  📓 The TAC Engineer's Troubleshooting Journal
</h3>

<p>Engineering in production means breaking things and solving real conflicts. During this implementation lab, I ran into two distinct runtime errors that provided vital architectural insights:</p>

<h4>
  
  
  🚨 1. Top-Level Schema Mismatch Failures (<code>Code: InvalidPolicyRule</code>)
</h4>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>The Challenge:</strong> The initial registration utility rejected the code payload, throwing a fatal syntax validation error pointing to a schema failure on the <code>"properties"</code> and <code>"mode"</code> parameters.</li>
<li>  <strong>The Root Cause:</strong> The <code>az policy definition create</code> engine expects the underlying <code>--rules</code> file configuration to start directly with the structural logic parameters (<code>if</code> and <code>then</code>). Wrapping these keys in metadata tags violates the parser's expected payload format.</li>
<li>  <strong>The Fix:</strong> Stripped the outer property layers out of the <code>allowed-skus.json</code> file completely, and passed meta properties like <code>--mode "Indexed"</code> out to explicit command-line flags.</li>
</ul>

<h4>
  
  
  🚨 2. Scope Binding Failures via Missing Context Containers (<code>Code: ResourceGroupNotFound</code>)
</h4>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>The Challenge:</strong> The policy assignment mapping crashed, returning a terminal exception indicating that the target resource group room could not be found.</li>
<li>  <strong>The Root Cause:</strong> Strict cost-control practices dictate tearing down all sandbox groups immediately after structural validations. Running an active policy assignment against an environment scope that doesn't exist crashes the engine call.</li>
<li>  <strong>The Fix:</strong> Refactored the command execution queue to explicitly guarantee the presence of the resource group container (<code>az group create</code>) <em>before</em> executing assignment mappings.</li>
</ul>




<h3>
  
  
  🚀 Live Workload Validation: The RequestDisallowedByPolicy Block
</h3>

<p>To prove the automated guardrails work perfectly under load, I simulated an accidental budget breach by forcing a deployment command for an unauthorized, high-tier enterprise instance shape (<code>Standard_D4s_v3</code>) directly against the protected resource group perimeter:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight shell"><code>az vm create <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--resource-group</span> <span class="s2">"Marathahalli_Lab_RG"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--name</span> <span class="s2">"Rogue_VM"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--image</span> <span class="s2">"Ubuntu2204"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--size</span> <span class="s2">"Standard_D4s_v3"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--admin-username</span> <span class="s2">"abhishek"</span> <span class="se">\</span>
  <span class="nt">--generate-ssh-keys</span>
</code></pre>

</div>



<h4>
  
  
  📸 Defensive Proof Point: The Wallet Secured
</h4>

<p>The deployment call spun for a brief moment, hit the ARM API gateway checkpoint, evaluated against the active assignment metadata constraints, and was violently rejected! The core control plane blocked resource generation immediately:<br>
</p>

<div class="highlight js-code-highlight">
<pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>azure.core.exceptions.HttpResponseError: (InvalidTemplateDeployment) The template deployment failed because of policy violation. 
Code: InvalidTemplateDeployment
Message: The template deployment failed because of policy violation. Please see details for more information.

Exception Details: (RequestDisallowedByPolicy) Resource 'Rogue_VM' was disallowed by policy 'Enforce_B_Series_Only'.
</code></pre>

</div>



<p><a href="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ftkp1wj7ub48c0yoq72gf.png" class="article-body-image-wrapper"><img src="https://media2.dev.to/dynamic/image/width=800%2Cheight=%2Cfit=scale-down%2Cgravity=auto%2Cformat=auto/https%3A%2F%2Fdev-to-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com%2Fuploads%2Farticles%2Ftkp1wj7ub48c0yoq72gf.png" alt=" " width="799" height="486"></a></p>




<h3>
  
  
  💡 Core FinOps &amp; AZ-104 Exam Lessons Learned
</h3>

<ul>
<li>  <strong>Deny vs. Audit Effects:</strong> The <code>deny</code> effect completely halts non-compliant resource allocation at the gate, protecting the budget instantly. The <code>audit</code> effect, conversely, allows deployments to succeed but flags them inside a compliance dashboard—ideal for mapping out production estates without creating application downtime risks.</li>
<li>  <strong>RBAC Scoping Precision:</strong> Security parameters inside custom role definitions require pinpoint precision. Explicitly matching actions to granular tasks ensures teams maintain access velocity without breaking zero-trust boundaries.</li>
</ul>

</description>

      <title>Agentic AI Security: Credentials and Permissions Define the Blast Radius</title>
      <dc:creator>Dwayne McDaniel</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Fri, 18 Sep 2026 07:19:45 +0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://dev.to/gitguardian/agentic-ai-security-credentials-and-permissions-define-the-blast-radius-4o3i</link>
      <guid>https://dev.to/gitguardian/agentic-ai-security-credentials-and-permissions-define-the-blast-radius-4o3i</guid>
      <description><h1>
  
  
  Agentic AI Security: Credentials and Permissions Define the Blast Radius
</h1>

<p>Prompt injection can't be patched away. Three 2026 agentic AI incidents show that credentials and permissions decide the damage.</p>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>The trick matters less than the access.</strong> Three 2026 disclosures, GitLost, Claude Code's CVE-2026-21852, and Amazon Q's CVE-2026-12957, show agent manipulation determines less damage than the credentials and permissions the agent can reach.</li>
<li>
<strong>Secrets exposure keeps climbing.</strong> GitGuardian found 28.6 million new hardcoded secrets on public GitHub in 2025 (up 34%), including 24,008 in MCP config files and 33,185 in the Shai-Hulud 2 breach alone.</li>
<li>
<strong>Reducing blast radius means covering the full lifecycle.</strong> GitGuardian blocks secrets at the model and tool boundary, discovers exposed credentials on developer endpoints, and speeds revocation so leaked keys lose value fast.</li>
</ul>

<p>In July 2026, researchers at Noma Labs coaxed GitHub's new Agentic Workflows into <a href="https://noma.security/blog/gitlost-how-we-tricked-githubs-ai-agent-into-leaking-private-repos/" rel="noopener noreferrer">leaking data from a private repository</a>. It wasn't from malware. They created a plausible-looking issue in a public repository containing instructions for the agent to retrieve information from other repositories in the organization. After testing variations of the prompt, they found that adding one word, "Additionally," was enough to get past GitHub's guardrails. The agent followed the instructions, fetched a private repository's README, and posted its contents as a public comment for anyone to read.</p>

<p>Most of the agentic AI security conversation fixates on that first part: the trick. Can an agent be manipulated into doing something its operator never intended? Yes, and GitLost shows how little it can take to bypass the safeguards designed to prevent it. But the trick only decides whether an incident starts. <strong>What the agent can reach determines how much damage follows</strong>. Across this year's most instructive agent incidents, the severity of the outcome came down to what the agent could access: credentials, permissions, and the authority attached to them.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Three agentic AI incidents with a single amplifier
</h2>

<p>Three disclosures from 2026 make the pattern hard to miss.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  #1. Claude Code: opening a repository was enough to lose an API key
</h3>

<p>In February, Check Point Research disclosed <a href="https://blog.checkpoint.com/research/check-point-researchers-expose-critical-claude-code-flaws/" rel="noopener noreferrer">three newly discovered ways developers could be exploited, including two new vulnerabilities in Anthropic's Claude Code</a>. Two allowed remote code execution through repository configuration files (.claude/settings.json and .mcp.json) that Claude Code could load when a developer started the tool inside an untrusted project. The third, CVE-2026-21852, worked differently but exposed something immediately useful to an attacker: the victim's Anthropic API key. A malicious repository could set the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL environment variable, and Claude Code would send API requests, credentials included, to the attacker's endpoint before it ever showed the user a trust prompt. Anthropic patched the three issues between August and December 2025, ahead of Check Point's February 2026 disclosure.</p>

<p>Notice what the attacker actually gets. The code execution flaws carried the higher severity scores, but the key exfiltration converts directly into durable access: authenticated API traffic redirected to attacker infrastructure, usage billed to the victim, and continued access wherever that API key remains valid. The exploit created the opening. But it was the stolen credential that extended the attacker's access.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  #2. Amazon Q: one config file inherited a full cloud identity
</h3>

<p>In June, Wiz Research disclosed <a href="https://www.wiz.io/blog/amazon-q-vulnerability" rel="noopener noreferrer">CVE-2026-12957 in the Amazon Q Developer extension</a> for Visual Studio Code. The extension automatically loaded Model Context Protocol (MCP) server configurations from a <code>.amazonq/mcp.json</code> file in any workspace a developer opened, without requiring consent or a workspace trust check. A developer could clone a malicious repository, open it with Amazon Q installed, and unknowingly launch an attacker-controlled MCP process.</p>

<p>The vulnerability gave the malicious MCP process a way in. What made it dangerous was the access that came with it: live AWS credentials from the developer's environment, including <code>AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID</code>, <code>AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY</code>, and active session tokens. Wiz's proof of concept used <code>aws sts get-caller-identity</code> to identify the AWS account and role available through those credentials, then sent that information to an external server. From there, an attacker could exercise whatever access those credentials allowed, potentially reaching production data, creating new access keys for persistence, or moving into internal systems.</p>

<p>Amazon fixed the consent flow in language server version <code>1.65.0</code>. But the broader lesson is about credential inheritance: the malicious configuration became dangerous because the process it launched inherited live credentials from the developer's environment.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  #3. GitLost: a blast radius without a stolen secret
</h3>

<p>GitLost, the GitHub Agentic Workflows vulnerability Noma Labs disclosed in July, shows the same problem from a different angle. The vulnerable workflow could read public issues while also holding read access to other repositories in the organization, including private ones. A crafted public issue manipulated the agent into using access it already had to retrieve information from a private repository. GitHub's guardrails were supposed to block that request, but a one-word change to the prompt was enough to bypass them.</p>

<p>This is what over-permissioning looks like in agentic systems. An agent can exercise permissions on behalf of whoever controls or influences its instructions, even if that person never possesses the underlying credential. GitLost therefore reinforces the same lesson as the Claude Code and Amazon Q incidents from the opposite direction: a credential does not have to be stolen for the access behind it to be abused. Whether an attacker steals an API key or manipulates an agent into using its existing repository access, the outcome depends on how much authority that agent has. In GitLost, the prompt injection started the incident, but excessive access determined what the attacker could reach.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Why agents concentrate the blast radius
</h2>

<p>None of this would matter as much if agents had little access to sensitive credentials and systems. The data shows the opposite.</p>

<p>GitGuardian's <a href="https://blog.gitguardian.com/the-state-of-secrets-sprawl-2026/" rel="noopener noreferrer">State of Secrets Sprawl 2026</a> found 28.6 million new hardcoded secrets pushed to public GitHub in 2025, up 34% year over year and the largest annual jump on record. Secrets tied to AI services are growing even faster, reaching 1,275,105 last year, an 81% increase.</p>

<p>Commits assisted by Claude Code also showed a 3.2% secret leak rate compared with a 1.5% baseline across all public commits. The report cautions against treating that gap as a failure of the tool itself, since developers still decide what gets pushed. The larger point is that AI-assisted development is happening in an environment where credential exposure is already widespread and increasing.</p>

<p>Agents add another layer of risk because they need access to other systems to be useful. That access is often provided through credentials such as database connection strings, cloud keys, SaaS tokens, and model API keys. Those credentials increasingly represent non-human identities with real authority across cloud infrastructure, developer tooling, SaaS platforms, and internal systems. And many of them are stored in plaintext on the same endpoints where agents operate: in .env files, ~/.aws directories, shell history, and MCP configuration files. GitGuardian found 24,008 unique secrets exposed in MCP-related config files on public GitHub, including 2,117 that were verified as valid. Quickstart guides that instruct developers to paste credentials directly into configuration files only add to that exposure.</p>

<p>The risk becomes even clearer at the endpoint level. When GitGuardian analyzed machines compromised by the <a href="https://blog.gitguardian.com/shai-hulud-2/" rel="noopener noreferrer">Shai-Hulud 2 supply chain attack</a>, 6,943 infected machines yielded 33,185 unique secrets, and 59% of those machines were CI/CD runners rather than personal laptops. That campaign did not need to manipulate an AI agent; the credentials already present on developer and CI environments were valuable enough on their own. Put a coding agent with file system and tool access on top of the same environment, and those credentials become accessible to a system that can read files, execute commands, call external services, and act on instructions. If that agent is compromised or manipulated, the credentials and permissions within its reach determine how far the attacker can go.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  Shrinking the blast radius before, during, and after compromise
</h2>

<p>Least privilege, isolation, approval gates, and egress controls remain essential. But coding agents also operate in environments full of credentials that grant access to cloud infrastructure, databases, APIs, developer tooling, and SaaS platforms. If those credentials are exposed, they can give an attacker access that persists long after the original agent interaction ends.</p>

<p>That makes secrets security a critical part of controlling an agent's blast radius. Limiting which credentials agents can discover, transmit, and continue using reduces what a successful manipulation can become. The challenge spans the full lifecycle: removing exposed credentials before an incident, stopping them from crossing model and tool boundaries during one, and quickly revoking them afterward. GitGuardian's secrets visibility and intelligence platform addresses each of those stages, including the developer and CI environments where coding agents actually run.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  Before: block credentials at the model and tool boundary
</h3>

<p>Once an agent is running, the goal shifts from removing credentials from its environment to preventing those credentials from moving through the agent unchecked. GitGuardian's AI Hooks register ggshield as a checkpoint inside Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, and Codex. Prompts are scanned before they reach the model, while file reads, shell commands, and MCP calls are checked before execution. If a secret is detected, the action is blocked and the finding is returned to the agent so it can self-correct and continue. Tool output is also scanned after execution, and the developer is alerted if sensitive material appears. All of this runs against the same 55600+ detectors used in pre-commit and CI.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.gitguardian.com/honeytoken" rel="noopener noreferrer">Honeytokens</a> add a tripwire on top. Place realistic-looking decoy credentials alongside real ones in configuration files and other locations an attacker or compromised agent is likely to inspect. If a laptop is compromised, a threat actor will often test the credentials it finds to see what they unlock. A compromised agent can also discover and attempt to use credentials available in its environment. The moment a honeytoken is used, GitGuardian triggers a real-time alert, exposing credential misuse even when the agent itself is the actor.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  During: remove what the agent can find
</h3>

<p>Reducing the blast radius starts with knowing which credentials are already within reach. Start by discovering the plaintext credentials AI workflows create and consume, scanning developer endpoints for credentials in <code>.env</code> files, cloud credential stores, MCP and agent configuration files, logs and shell history. Pair that with an inventory of which agents and <a href="https://blog.gitguardian.com/mcp-governance-framework/" rel="noopener noreferrer">MCP servers</a> are running across the fleet and what they can reach.</p>

<p>GitGuardian's <a href="https://www.gitguardian.com/developer-endpoint-protection" rel="noopener noreferrer">Developer Endpoint Protection</a> does both through your existing Mobile Device Management (MDM) tooling, using scheduled scans with no continuous agent and the same <a href="https://www.gitguardian.com/ggshield" rel="noopener noreferrer">ggshield</a> detection engine already widely used in developer workflows. For organizations already running ggshield in pre-commit, extending that protection to developer endpoints is a configuration change within the existing MDM deployment, not a new agent or infrastructure project. Every credential removed from an endpoint before an incident is blast radius an attacker never gets.</p>

<p>Credentials are only half the equation. GitGuardian also maps which permissions and identities each credential is tied to, so an agent that can read one key isn't treated the same as an agent that can read a key with production access. The same credential found on an endpoint and in a secrets manager becomes a higher-priority finding than either alone, because it signals broader reach, not just exposure.</p>

<h3>
  
  
  After: revoke faster than the attacker can move
</h3>

<p>Leaked credentials stay dangerous long after an incident scrolls out of the news cycle: <a href="https://www.gitguardian.com/state-of-secrets-sprawl-report-2026" rel="noopener noreferrer">64% of secrets confirmed valid in 2022</a> were still valid and unrevoked in January 2026. That persistence makes rapid response especially important in agentic environments, where credentials can be discovered and exfiltrated quickly.</p>

<p>Knowing a secret leaked is not enough. You need to know whether it is still valid, what it unlocks, and who owns it. GitGuardian enriches incidents with available validity, ownership, scope, and location context. That turns "an agent may have read a key" into a prioritized list of credentials that need investigation or revocation. For secrets found in code or CI, GitGuardian can push them directly into your secrets manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, CyberArk, Akeyless); where the provider supports it, GitGuardian can revoke the credential directly rather than walking you through manual steps. GitGuardian customers remediated five times more secrets in 2025 than in 2024. When a credential has been exposed, fast revocation removes the authority the attacker can continue to exercise.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The blast radius is defined by what the agent can reach
</h2>

<p>The GitLost writeup closes with two recommendations that get to the heart of the issue: never treat user-controlled content as trusted instruction input, and scope permissions to the minimum required. Security teams cannot fully prevent agents from being manipulated, but they can control the credentials, permissions, and authority those agents have access to. That is where the blast radius is decided. The next prompt injection may be as trivial as "Additionally." Whether it exposes a README, a cloud credential, or something more consequential depends on how much authority the agent had in the first place.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  FAQ
</h2>

<p><strong>What is prompt injection, and how did it play out in the GitLost incident?</strong></p>

<p>In July 2026, Noma Labs researchers tricked GitHub's Agentic Workflows into leaking a private repository. A crafted public issue told the agent to retrieve data from other repositories, and adding one word, "Additionally," bypassed GitHub's guardrails. The agent fetched a private README and posted it publicly. The trick started the incident; the agent's existing repository access decided how much data leaked.</p>

<p><strong>How can organizations prevent prompt injection attacks against AI agents?</strong></p>

<p>Two controls matter most: never treat user-controlled content as trusted instructions, and scope agent permissions to the minimum required. GitGuardian's AI Hooks apply the first control by scanning prompts, file reads, shell commands, and MCP calls before execution in tools like Claude Code and Cursor, blocking detected secrets. Teams can't stop every manipulation, but they can control what the agent can reach.</p>

<p><strong>Who is responsible for AI agent security?</strong></p>

<p>Vendors patch the disclosed flaw: Anthropic fixed Claude Code's three issues, including CVE-2026-21852, between August and December 2025, and Amazon fixed Amazon Q's consent flow in language server 1.65.0. But patching doesn't remove the exposure. Responsibility for limiting access, least-privilege scoping, credential discovery, and fast revocation, sits with the organization running the agent.</p>

<p><strong>What happens if an AI coding agent's API key or credentials get leaked?</strong></p>

<p>In the Claude Code case (CVE-2026-21852), a malicious repo could redirect API requests, credentials included, to an attacker's endpoint before any trust prompt appeared, enabling continued access and billing to the victim. In the Amazon Q case (CVE-2026-12957), a malicious MCP process inherited live AWS credentials. GitGuardian found 64% of secrets valid in 2022 were still unrevoked by January 2026.</p>

<p><strong>What is a honeytoken, and how does it help catch a compromised AI agent?</strong></p>

<p>A honeytoken is a decoy credential that looks real. It sits alongside genuine credentials in files an attacker or compromised agent is likely to check. Attackers often test credentials found on a compromised device to see what they unlock, and a compromised agent can do the same. The moment a honeytoken is used, GitGuardian triggers a real-time alert, exposing the misuse.</p>

<p><strong>How do you limit the "blast radius" of a compromised AI agent?</strong></p>

<p>Blast radius reduction means covering credentials before, during, and after an incident: discovering exposed secrets in .env files and MCP configs (GitGuardian found 24,008 in public MCP config files alone), blocking secrets at the model and tool boundary during execution, and revoking leaks fast. GitGuardian customers remediated five times more secrets in 2025 than in 2024.</p>

      <title>Stop Paying $500/mo for APM: The 5-Script Monitoring Stack That Covers 90% of It</title>
      <dc:creator>Hive80-lab</dc:creator>
      <pubDate>Thu, 17 Sep 2026 15:40:23 +0000</pubDate>

      <guid>https://dev.to/hive80lab/stop-paying-500mo-for-apm-the-5-script-monitoring-stack-that-covers-90-of-it-34kb</guid>
      <description><p>Last month I audited a client's monitoring bill: <strong>$540/month</strong> for an APM platform that three engineers had partially configured — and two of them had left the company.</p>

<p>The dashboard was pretty. It was also wrong: it monitored endpoints nobody hit anymore, missed the actual money-path API entirely, and had alert rules that paged the whole team every time a batch job ran.</p>

<p>Here's the uncomfortable math: for most small-to-mid teams, 90% of the value of a $500/month APM subscription comes from five boring checks you can run with free scripts. You keep paying for the other 10% out of habit.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What the $540 actually bought (and what it should have)
</h2>

<p>The essentials that generate real signal:</p>

<ol>
<li>
<strong>Heartbeat check on the money path.</strong> One curl to your critical endpoint every 60s, alert on 2 consecutive failures. Distinguishes "slow" from "dead."</li>
<li>
<strong>Disk + memory guard.</strong> The #1 silent killer of small deployments. 5 lines of shell, runs in cron.</li>
<li>
<strong>Log-noise tripwire.</strong> Grep yesterday's logs for ERROR/Traceback counts vs. 7-day baseline. Rising trend = someone should look <em>today</em>.</li>
<li>
<strong>SSL + domain expiry.</strong> Nothing humbles a team like a site outage because a cert expired. Free to prevent.</li>
<li>
<strong>Dead-man's-switch on your own jobs.</strong> Your backups and cron jobs should check in when they succeed — and scream when they don't.</li>
</ol>

<p>That's it. That's the stack. Run it from a $5 VPS.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  The part nobody tells you: the checks are easy, the <em>system</em> is hard
</h2>

<p>Scripts aren't the product. The product is:</p>

<ul>
<li>knowing <strong>which endpoint is the money path</strong> (hint: it's rarely the homepage),</li>
<li>alert rules that don't cry wolf (2-failure minimum, severity tiers),</li>
<li>a runbook that says what to <em>do</em> at 2AM, not just "error detected,"</li>
<li>a weekly pulse review: what alerted, what was noise, what did we fix?</li>
</ul>

<p>That discipline layer is where most teams fail — and it's exactly why they end up paying $500/month for someone else to have opinions about it.</p>

<h2>
  
  
  What I actually recommend
</h2>

<p>If you have a platform team: fine, keep your APM, but make sure it does the 5 checks above <em>correctly</em> — most don't.</p>

<p>If you're a small team drowning in dashboards: rip it out, run the 5-script stack, and reinvest the $6k/year into the thing that actually earns money.</p>

Both are one-time purchases, no subscription, and they fit in a single afternoon to deploy.</p>
